summary: Sets out requirements for a Media Server Control Protocol that lets an application server use a media server. It covers services such as announcements, interactive voice response, and conferencing. The document says the logical roles existed in IETF work but the protocol between them had not been defined. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5167 describes what a protocol should let an application server ask a media server to do. Its requirements cover calls, conferences, announcements, and interactive voice services.

questions: application server to media server protocol
what is a media server control protocol
what is an application server vs media server
subtitle: Requirements for a control protocol between application servers and media servers

tldr.problem: IETF conferencing work described application servers and media servers but did not define their control protocol.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5167 lists requirements for a Media Server Control Protocol covering announcements, conferencing, interactive voice response, and operations.
tldr.outcome: This Informational document sets requirements, not a protocol specification. It leaves detailed protocol and security design to related framework and protocol work.

today: RFC 5167 is an Informational requirements document published in March 2008. The supplied metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and it does not define the control protocol.

sections.title: Application and Media Server Roles
sections.content:
An Application Server (AS) hosts communication applications and controls services. A Media Server (MS) processes real-time media, for example by playing announcements, mixing streams, detecting telephone key tones, or transcoding audio or video.

RFC 5167 sets requirements for a protocol between these logical entities. It covers the protocol rather than defining the functions of the AS or MS, and it does not specify distributed media-processing algorithms.
sections.plainLanguage: The application server decides what should happen in a call. The media server performs tasks such as playing audio, detecting button presses, or mixing participants' streams.

sections.title: General Media Control Requirements
sections.content:
The control protocol should let one or more application servers request services from one or more media servers over a reliable transport. It should support conferencing and interactive voice response, with audio, tones, text, and video.

The protocol should support requests, responses, and notifications. SIP and SDP establish and modify media connections. An optional broker or proxy may help connect servers, but the protocol must not require one.
sections.plainLanguage: The application server sends a request, the media server replies, and the media server can also report events. The control channel needs reliable delivery.

sections.title: Mixing, Interactive Voice, and Operations
sections.content:
The requirements include controlling volume and muting, playing announcements to one person or a conference, and creating or changing mixing, announcement, and interactive voice sessions. An application server should be able to define a conference mix and video layout, and learn which media layouts the server supports.

For interactive voice response, the application server should be able to run scripts, collect results such as telephone keypad input, and manage later steps. The application server also needs to inspect active session state, and the media server needs to report its status.
sections.plainLanguage: The application server can request an announcement, change a conference mix, or collect keypad input. It also needs ways to check the media server's active sessions and status.

sections.title: Authorization and Resource Protection
sections.content:
The requirements call for authentication so that application servers and media servers can verify each other. The control channel must protect the confidentiality and integrity of its data, and the protocol should prevent unauthorized operations.

Because several application servers may use one media server, one server's resources must be protected from another. RFC 5167 leaves detailed security procedures to the framework and protocol documents, while noting that existing SIP security mechanisms may be used.
sections.plainLanguage: Only authorized servers should control media sessions. A media server must keep one application's resources separate from another application's resources.
